title: Streaming Data Speciality Exam
description: 20 questions drawn from a pool of 26, covering streaming concepts and the PDI streaming pattern across MQTT, Kafka, and AMQP. Pass mark is 80%. Open-book — browse any page, hover glossary terms, or ask the AI assistant. Your answers are saved as you go. Explanations appear after submission.

questions.prompt: What most fundamentally distinguishes streaming data from batch data?
options: Streaming data is always smaller in volume than batch data
Streaming data is an unbounded sequence of events processed as it arrives, rather than a finite dataset processed all at once
Streaming data can only be stored in time-series databases
Streaming data does not require any transformation before loading
questions.explanation: Batch processing works on a bounded chunk and ends when the data is exhausted. Streaming data is unbounded — the consumer keeps running and processes events on the fly as they arrive.

questions.prompt: In PDI's streaming pattern, what is the role of the parent transformation?
options: It parses the JSON payload of each message
It holds the streaming consumer step, which collects incoming messages into batches and hands each batch to a child transformation
It writes the final records to the target database
It runs only once at startup to create the broker
questions.explanation: The parent transformation contains the consumer step (MQTT/Kafka/AMQP Consumer). It batches incoming messages and invokes the child transformation per batch; the child does the parsing and loading.

questions.prompt: Why must 'Get records from stream' be the first step in the child transformation?
options: Because it is alphabetically first in the step list
Because it produces rows and so cannot be placed mid-stream; rows must originate at the start of the stream
Because it requires a database connection that must open before any other step
Because it deletes the previous batch before processing
questions.explanation: 'Get records from stream' produces rows from the batched messages. A row-producing step must be the first step in a stream — to add the data to an existing stream you would join it in instead.

questions.scenario: A consumer step is configured with Duration (ms) = 5000 and Number of records = 100, consuming a topic that produces roughly one message per second.
questions.prompt: What triggers a batch to be sent to the child transformation, and which threshold usually fires first here?
options: Only the record count; it fires first
Whichever threshold is reached first; at ~1 msg/sec the 5-second duration usually fires first, sending ~5 records
Both thresholds must be satisfied simultaneously
Only the duration; the record count is ignored
questions.explanation: A batch flushes when the first of the two thresholds is met. At ~1 msg/sec, the 5-second window is reached long before 100 records accumulate, so each batch carries about 5 records.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are streaming protocols supported by PDI's streaming steps? (Select all that apply.)
options: MQTT
Kafka
AMQP
SMTP
questions.explanation: PDI provides consumer steps for MQTT, Kafka, AMQP (and JMS/Kinesis). SMTP is an email transfer protocol, not a streaming source.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of the publish/subscribe model used by streaming brokers?
options: Producers must wait for each consumer to acknowledge before sending the next message
Producers and consumers are decoupled — neither needs to know about the other; any number of subscribers can receive a topic
Only one consumer can ever read a given topic
Messages are delivered in random order to balance load
questions.explanation: In pub/sub, producers publish to a topic and any number of subscribers register interest. The decoupling lets producers and consumers scale and evolve independently.

questions.prompt: Which two batch settings act as backpressure controls to stop a fast stream overwhelming the consumer? (Select all that apply.)
options: Message prefetch limit
Maximum concurrent batches
Target table name
Commit comment
questions.explanation: The message prefetch limit caps how many messages PDI queues in memory, and maximum concurrent batches bounds parallel batch processing. Together they manage throughput versus resource use.

questions.prompt: Why is MQTT well suited to IoT and sensor networks?
options: It encrypts every message with a hardware security module
It is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol that needs minimal resources, suiting constrained devices
It guarantees messages are never duplicated under any configuration
It stores all historical data on the device itself
questions.explanation: MQTT's minimal overhead lets small microcontrollers communicate reliably with low power and cost, which is exactly what IoT devices need.

questions.prompt: What does MQTT QoS level 2 (exactly once) trade off compared with QoS 0?
options: It is faster but can lose messages
It guarantees each message is delivered exactly once, at the cost of the highest overhead
It disables the broker's persistence entirely
It is identical to QoS 0 but renamed
questions.explanation: QoS 0 is lowest latency but can lose messages; QoS 1 can duplicate; QoS 2 guarantees exactly-once delivery but carries the most overhead.

questions.prompt: In the HiveMQ workshop, which port does the broker expose for the MQTT TCP listener?
questions.explanation: HiveMQ exposes the MQTT TCP listener on 1883 (Control Center on 9090). 18083 is the EMQX dashboard and 5672 is the AMQP port.

questions.scenario: An MQTT producer and consumer are both connected to EMQX, but the child transformation never runs and no output files are written.
questions.prompt: Which are sensible first things to check? (Select all that apply.)
options: Producer and consumer use the same topic
The consumer batch has Duration (ms) or Number of records set greater than 0
The child transformation starts with Get records from stream
The broker has been uninstalled to reset its state
questions.explanation: No output usually means a topic mismatch, a batch with no trigger threshold (so it never flushes), or a child transformation that does not begin with Get records from stream. Uninstalling the broker is not a troubleshooting step.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the MQTT 'clean session' flag being set to false?
options: It deletes all retained messages on connect
The broker persists the client's subscriptions and queued QoS 1/2 messages between connections
It forces QoS 0 for all messages
It disables the consumer's child transformation
questions.explanation: With clean session false, the broker keeps the client's state — subscriptions and queued QoS 1/2 messages — so they survive a disconnect. True means no state is retained.

questions.prompt: In the EMQX logistics workshop, what does the child transformation ultimately produce?
options: A single aggregated row inserted into Kafka
Minor and major alert rows appended to output files
A new MQTT topic for each truck
A schema registered with the Schema Registry
questions.explanation: The EMQX child transformation resolves the sensor type, filters minor and major alerts, aggregates them, and appends results to major_alert.txt and minor_alert.txt.

questions.prompt: What does Kafka's KRaft mode change about cluster operation?
options: It adds a second ZooKeeper cluster for redundancy
It manages cluster metadata within Kafka itself using the Raft protocol, removing the ZooKeeper dependency
It disables partitions in favour of a single log
It requires every broker to also be a Schema Registry
questions.explanation: KRaft (Kafka Raft metadata mode) consolidates metadata management inside Kafka via Raft consensus, eliminating ZooKeeper and simplifying deployment and scaling.

questions.prompt: What is a Kafka offset?
options: The time in milliseconds to wait before reading
A sequential ID that uniquely identifies a record within a partition
The number of consumers in a group
The size of the message in bytes
questions.explanation: Each record within a partition has a monotonically increasing offset. Consumers track offsets to know what they have read and where to resume.

questions.prompt: What does setting auto.offset.reset to 'earliest' do for a consumer with no committed offset?
options: Starts reading only new messages produced after it connects
Starts reading from the beginning of the topic
Resets all partitions to offset zero on every batch
Skips the first record of every partition
questions.explanation: With no committed offset, 'earliest' reads from the start of the topic; 'latest' would read only messages produced after the consumer connects.

questions.scenario: In the user-events workshop, String fields loaded to MySQL end up as TINYTEXT and break index creation.
questions.prompt: How is this fixed in the child transformation?
options: By switching the Table output step to a Text file output
By setting explicit data-type lengths for each field on the Select values Metadata tab so PDI generates VARCHAR
By disabling the primary key on the MySQL table
By converting all fields to Integer
questions.explanation: Without explicit lengths, PDI maps String fields to TINYTEXT, which cannot be indexed. Setting lengths on the Select values Metadata tab makes PDI emit VARCHAR of the right size.

questions.prompt: Why is a Formula step (not a Calculator step) used to convert register_time from epoch milliseconds to seconds?
options: The Calculator step cannot output Integer values
The Calculator step requires both operands to be stream fields, while Formula supports an inline constant like 1000
The Formula step runs faster on streaming data
MySQL rejects values produced by the Calculator step
questions.explanation: Calculator needs both operands as existing fields — you cannot type a literal 1000. Formula supports inline constants, so [register_time_epoch] / 1000 works directly.

questions.prompt: When configuring the Table output step for MySQL in this workshop, why should the Target schema be left blank?
options: MySQL does not support the Table output step
MySQL uses the database name from the connection; setting a schema qualifies the table (e.g. kafka_warehouse.user_events) and can fail
Leaving it blank truncates the table on every run
A blank schema enables Avro serialization
questions.explanation: For MySQL the database comes from the connection itself. Setting Target schema causes PDI to qualify the table name, which can fail or behave unexpectedly.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a Kafka consumer group?
options: It encrypts messages for the group's members
Its members share the work of reading a topic, each being assigned a subset of the topic's partitions
It stores the schema for every topic the group reads
It guarantees exactly-once delivery across all topics
questions.explanation: Consumers in a group cooperate: each is assigned a subset of partitions so the group divides the load of consuming a topic.

questions.prompt: In AMQP, where does a producer send a message?
options: Directly to a queue
To an exchange, which routes it to queues using bindings and routing keys
To the consumer's IP address
To the Schema Registry
questions.explanation: AMQP producers publish to an exchange, not a queue directly. The exchange uses bindings and routing keys to decide which queues receive the message.

questions.prompt: What does a 'fanout' exchange do?
options: Routes a message to exactly one queue based on the routing key
Broadcasts every message it receives to all bound queues, ignoring routing keys
Stores messages on disk only
Converts JSON messages to Avro
questions.explanation: Fanout is the default exchange type. It ignores routing keys and broadcasts each message to every queue bound to it.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics can an AMQP queue be configured with? (Select all that apply.)
options: Durable (survives broker restarts)
Exclusive (used by a single connection)
Auto-delete (removed when its consumer count drops to zero)
Encrypted-at-rest by the routing key
questions.explanation: Queues can be durable, exclusive, and/or auto-delete. There is no 'encrypted by routing key' property — routing keys determine routing, not encryption.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended order of operations when first using the AMQP Consumer step to create a new queue?
options: Start the producer first, then run the consumer
Run the AMQP Consumer step first to initialize the broker bindings, then start producing messages
Delete any existing exchange before running either
Run the producer and consumer simultaneously from the same transformation
questions.explanation: As a best practice, run the AMQP Consumer first so the queue and bindings are initialized, then start the producer — otherwise early messages may have nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: In the RabbitMQ workshop, what default port does the broker use for AMQP connections, and what for its management UI?
options: 1883 for AMQP, 9090 for the UI
5672 for AMQP, 15672 for the management UI
9092 for AMQP, 3000 for the UI
18083 for AMQP, 8080 for the UI
questions.explanation: RabbitMQ listens on 5672 for AMQP and serves its management UI on 15672 (default credentials guest/guest).

questions.prompt: What happens if you point the AMQP Consumer at an existing queue whose settings differ from those it would create?
options: PDI silently overwrites the queue's settings
The transformation aborts
The message is rerouted to a fanout exchange
The consumer creates a second queue with a suffix
questions.explanation: If the named queue already exists with different parameters (or a different exchange type), the transformation aborts rather than silently changing the broker configuration.
